description.en: One memory plugin instead of three: 8 unified memory_* tools and a single 1,235-character injection, with meow-memory's seven-layer SQLite as the main store and a rebuildable graph index. Tool schemas 56,759 B → 13,567 B (−76.1%), standing prompt 4,085 → 1,235 chars (−69.8%). Nothing was dropped: writes land in the main store first, graph links that cannot be written are queued instead of lost, and the setting page takes effect without a restart. 0.4.0 adds query decomposition, write-time consolidation, supersede + inflation checks, an entity layer on the graph, and co-occurrence query expansion learned from your own keywords — every one of them has an off switch and an on/off reading. 0.5.0 bridges CJK word forms so a paraphrase still lands. 0.6.0 makes scoring scale-adaptive: on a 660-entry snapshot, verbatim hit@1 0.895 → 0.921 and paraphrased 0.333 → 0.417 with zero wrong flips, and every hit now carries its `status`. 0.6.1 turns the three-trees-out-of-sync problem into one command (`tools/sync-trees.mjs`, dry-run by default, never deletes), pins the adaptive-idf wiring with two static regexes so a silent behaviour regression cannot pass green, and fixes a `%20` path bug in a maintenance script — engine bytes unchanged. 0.6.2 fixes a recall bug where the store said nothing when something was there: the noise floor dropped the only matchable word and left a word that does not exist in the store in its place (8 of 1,531 English questions came back empty). It now rescues only the words the noise floor dropped and never function words, so empty replies went 0.52% → 0 while hit@1/5/10/20, MRR and the 660-entry snapshot readings stayed bit-identical. 0.6.3 makes answers reproducible: a tie on score used to fall back to corpus order (V8's stable sort), so the same question could give two different top-tens depending on how the store happened to lay the rows out. The ladder now ends with updated-later-first and a natural id order, the adaptive-idf cluster pick no longer breaks ties by array index, and no ordering step uses localeCompare — and every reading stayed bit-identical. 0.6.4 fixes single-character queries: the tokenizer only emits CJK bigrams, so a one-hanzi question yields no tokens and the retrieval gate treated “cannot tokenize” as “not in memory” — the most direct questions (`读`, `钱`, `花`) always came back empty. It now falls back to a literal substring pass over title/content/keywords only when the query is a single CJK code point and tokenization produced nothing, still going through the same ordering ladder; English stopwords and punctuation stay closed. Every reading is bit-identical — this restores reachability, not ranking. 0.6.5 fixes punctuated single-character queries: the 0.6.4 gate demanded exactly one code point, yet a one-hanzi question almost always carries punctuation — `读？`, `钱。`, `花！`, `「读」` all came back empty. The gate now strips punctuation and whitespace first and requires exactly one remaining hanzi, allowing only punctuation/whitespace beside it; letters, digits and symbols stay closed, and a repeated character counts once. Every reading is bit-identical again — reachability, not ranking. 0.6.6 fixes dirty memories: `...d.keywords` in `docText` threw `TypeError: d.keywords is not iterable` for entries whose keywords were missing, null, or a comma-joined string (imported rows, rows written by other plugins, caller-built docs) — not one missing hit, but a whole failed search. Keywords now go through `kwList`: arrays, comma/ideographic-comma strings and JSON strings all count, and `docText`, the scoring fields `kwToks`/`kwSets`, `keywordHitScore` and the index signature all use it (comma-joined keywords finally reach tf-idf). Every reading is bit-identical — reachability again, not ranking. 0.6.7 fixes broken rows: a single null / undefined / scalar entry in `docs` (half-written rows, truncated imports, a caller passing ids instead of objects) made `docText` throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'title')`, and a non-array `docs` died on `docs.length`. Both entry points now pass a gate `liveDocs(docs)`: non-arrays return empty, entries are checked for object-ness, filtering happens only when something is broken, and a clean array is returned as the same reference (the index cache is keyed by a content signature, not identity, so nothing is invalidated); an all-broken array returns empty rather than scoring null as a memory. Every reading is bit-identical. 0.6.8 is about the lifetime of the checks themselves: versions, suite counts, assertion totals and time budgets all advance every release, so writing them as equality turns every bump into a false failure (`0.2.31→35` hit it four times; `0.6.2→0.6.7` hand-bumped `steps.length === 35 → 36` each time and edited two hand-copied doc numbers). Suite count is now a floor (`SUITE_FLOOR`: adding a suite needs no edit, losing one fails immediately), the current numbers in the docs are reconciled automatically against the baseline totals, historical milestones keep their own numbers, and the version ladder is compared by version, not layout. The engine is byte-identical; every reading is the same. 0.6.9 measures the ruler first: since 0.3.0 every published reading came from a single pass in a single order (corpus in storage order, questions in fixture order), and those single-pass numbers are exactly what rejected three candidates (English stemming, MMR, coverage re-rank). If the ruler is order-sensitive, those negatives carry the ruler own noise. `tools/probe-rigor.mjs` now pins seven properties: three consecutive passes give bit-identical readings (std = 0), reversed corpus order, three shuffles (seed 3/11/42), reversed question order, a second independent scorer, an injected same-score-corpus-order bias that must go red (A/B top-1 hits 23 to 15), and fixed tier sizes 45/14/10. On 69 real-corpus questions: hit@1 0.9565 / hit@3 0.9855 / MRR 0.9686, unchanged across passes and orders. The engine is byte-identical; LoCoMo and real-corpus readings are unchanged. 0.6.10 removes a fixed per-query cost: the search-index cache key is a content signature, and while the usual answer is that the store did not change, the price was paid in full every time. On four isomorphic corpora (660 / 2,000 / 5,000 / 10,000) the signature consumed 28.8%-30.6% of a warm search (0.96 / 2.84 / 7.04 / 14.16 ms). It is now accounted per document: a WeakMap keyed by the doc holds a 32-bit per-doc hash plus a snapshot of the fields that feed it, compared by value (not object identity) before reuse; the per-doc hash had to be lifted out of the rolling value to be cacheable at all; shapes whose values cannot be compared fall back to direct computation. Signatures now cost 0.062 / 0.189 / 0.528 / 1.198 ms (15x, share down to 2.8%-3.5%) and a warm search 3.24 to 2.18, 9.67 to 6.80, 23.0 to 15.3, 49.2 to 37.6 ms. Ranking is byte-identical; LoCoMo and real-corpus readings are unchanged. 0.6.11 keeps paying down fixed cost: the remaining warm-search time is now accounted per channel, and the most expensive one is verbatim matching, which used to rebuild one lowercased string of the whole store on every query (id + project + title + content + keywords) just to answer whether an identifier appears verbatim, 2.03 MB at 10,000 docs and 35.7%-50.6% of a warm search; splitting that further showed 5.78 ms spent building strings against 0.51 ms of actual scanning. The haystack now lives in the index next to the token table, is built per document on demand and accounted (built / reused), and nothing is built when the query carries no identifier. The same change closed a 0.6.10 hole: the haystack contains project, project was never part of the signature, and once the string is cached a changed project would have been served from a stale index. Warm search: 2.04 to 1.62, 5.04 to 4.20, 11.88 to 9.12, 24.45 to 18.82 ms (-20.6% / -16.7% / -23.2% / -23.0%), verbatim share down to 18.6%-34.9%. Ranking is byte-identical; LoCoMo and real-corpus readings are unchanged. 0.6.12 keeps paying down fixed cost and targets the final ordering step. After the signature accounting of 0.6.10 and the verbatim accounting of 0.6.11, --cpu-prof attributed the largest remaining block to bandize (10,000 docs, 300 queries): to hand back the top ten it sorted the full hit list twice, once by _raw to assign bands and once by band, score, update time and id for the final order, while all three call sites only take the first k afterwards. Ordering was 40.3% of a warm search, about 11 ms per query, more than scanning documents. Band numbers are now written on the hit itself instead of a per-query Map, the comparator is factored into one orderOf ladder (band, then score, then more recently updated first, then natural id order) shared by both the full sort and the heap, and bandize takes a limit and selects the top k with a bounded max heap whose root is the worst selected hit; when the wanted count is not smaller than the total, the original full sort runs unchanged, so small stores and large k behave bit for bit as before. Bands and explain.band are only written on the surviving hits, and the temporary field is deleted. Search 27.377 to 19.985 ms (-27.0%), the production searchAdaptive path 31.086 to 23.097 ms (-25.7%), ordering share 40.3% to 21.5% (orderOf itself 0.9%), index reuse still 0.751 ms per query and cold index build unchanged at 270.7 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: the top k matches full-sort-then-slice across 500 random corpora and six k values, the total returned count stays 1,500, and LoCoMo plus the 52-question real-corpus readings are unchanged. 0.6.13 keeps paying down fixed cost and targets band assignment. After 0.6.12 capped ordering at the top k, a fresh --cpu-prof run (10,000 docs, 300 queries, 19.99 ms per search) showed the largest remaining block was still the full sort that exists only to assign bands: hits.slice().sort((a, b) => b[rawKey] - a[rawKey]) inside bandize, 21.5% of a warm search (bandize 10.9% plus the internal raw comparator 10.6%), paying comparator calls and object field reads for entries that can never reach the top k. Bands depend only on the distinct raw values after sorting, so the fix is three steps with identical semantics: copy raw values into a Float64Array and sort it with the native numeric sort (no comparator), walk it downward once to build a threshold chain (a0 is the maximum, a(i+1) is the largest value below 0.85 times a(i)), then binary-search each hit own value against the chain, where its band equals m minus 1 minus lo. Fallback: when any raw value is not a finite non-negative number (NaN, undefined, null, negative), the strictly decreasing anchor premise fails (0.85 times a negative value is larger, not smaller), so the whole pass falls back to the 0.6.13-era full sort setBandsBySort, and identified hits keep band minus one and stay out of the chain. Search 19.985 to 16.329 ms (-18.3%), the production searchAdaptive path 23.097 to 18.812 ms (-18.6%), band assignment share 21.5% to 7.8% (threshold chain 7.0% plus bandize 0.8%), index reuse still 0.703 ms per query, cold build 259 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty answers, and the 52-question real-corpus readings match 0.6.12 exactly. 0.6.14 removes the leftovers from the hot path. After 0.6.13 cut band assignment from 21.5% to 7.8%, the function view only showed work being done (search self 45.8%, scanDoc 17.8%); a line-level attribution over cpuprofile positionTicks exposed the real cost: delete h._lv alone accounted for 791.5 ms, with delete h._vb and delete h._sr adding another 353 ms, so 1.14 s of a 5,671.8 ms sample went into removing values that had just been attached. The cause is four use-then-unset temporaries on each hit object (verbatim hit, pattern ratio, level intent, assertion density) that were cleaned up with delete, and delete pushes an object into dictionary mode, so every later property access, including the h._raw read inside the freshly optimized bandize, goes through a hash table; four saved assignments bought a slower whole path. Two changes keep semantics identical: the four temporaries move into parallel arrays indexed like hits (pushed right next to hits.push, read back by index), leaving the returned field set exactly as before; and idf is memoized per pass (within one pass idf is constant per term, so a per-query cache with idfAt yields bit-identical values without recomputing Math.log), with the cache reset when adaptive idf swaps its ruler. Two per-query allocations also disappear: raw.slice is only kept when explain is on, and the Math.max spread becomes a loop that preserves NaN propagation. Search 16.329 to 11.567 ms (-29.2%), or -57.7% against 27.377 ms in 0.6.12; the production searchAdaptive path 18.812 to 13.520 ms (-28.1%); zero delete calls left on the hot path, index reuse 0.679 ms per query, cold build 275 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty answers, and the 52-question real-corpus readings match 0.6.13 exactly. 0.6.15 stops recomputing coverage per candidate. After 0.6.14 removed the 1.14 s of delete work, the function view again only showed work being done (search self 40.6%, scanDoc 18.8%); the line view named the cost: inside scanDoc the most expensive line was coverage, the loop that walks the query terms for every candidate and adds the idf of each term the document contains, at 573.9 ms over 300 queries, or 1.9 ms per query. The quantity itself is simple, the share of the query covered by a document, weighted by idf, but the algorithm was two-dimensional: for each candidate (up to 10,000) the full query vocabulary (dozens of terms) was asked again through a Map, hundreds of thousands of hash lookups per query just to produce 10,000 numbers, while the inverted index already records which documents each term appears in. Four changes keep semantics identical: per-query term idf is computed once into two Float64Arrays and read directly by the scoring loop; coverage is accumulated along the inverted index (a zero table sized by the document count, filled in the original query-term order, leaving one clamped division inside scanDoc), and because the addition order is unchanged every candidate keeps a bit-identical floating-point sum; when the inverted index is absent (explicitly disabled, or the query carries identifiers) the old per-candidate lookup path returns unchanged; and the candidate loop takes one record reference up front instead of re-resolving the same fields. The adaptive-idf ruler swap now re-accumulates both accounts in a fixed order: clear the idf cache, refresh term weights, rebuild the coverage table, then rescan. Search 11.567 to 10.673 ms (-7.8%), or -61.0% against 27.377 ms in 0.6.12; the production searchAdaptive path 13.520 to 12.522 ms (-7.4%); the coverage line 573.9 to 14.9 ms and scanDoc self time 23.8% to 18.8%; index reuse 0.698 ms per query and cold build 271 ms are flat within noise. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty answers, and all 52 real-corpus questions keep their scores and the two rank swaps. 0.6.16 stops looking up the term table for every candidate. After 0.6.15 removed the 573.9 ms of coverage work, the function view again only showed work being done (search self 48.0 percent, sigDocOf 9.5 percent, banding 7.5 percent); the line view named the next cost: the scoring loop that asks a Map for each query term of each candidate, 535.3 ms over 300 queries, about 1.8 ms per query. The quantity is term frequency times rarity times whether the hit was in the title or the keywords, and the first two inputs are fixed at index time; the inverted index already records which documents each term appears in. Three changes keep semantics identical: the inverted value grows from a list of document indexes to three parallel lists (index, term frequency, field-hit bits), with frequency and bits pushed in the same document-loop order so they stay index-aligned, and field weights are never multiplied into the index because they are per-query options that callers can override, so only the hit bits are stored and the weight is applied on the hot path; scoring runs the other way round, first preparing per-candidate constants (coverage, the length-normalisation denominator, the coordination term) and then, in the original query-term order, letting each term touch only the documents that contain it, adding its saturated term score to the raw score, so every candidate receives its addends in the same order and keeps a bit-identical floating-point sum; the finishing pass then applies synonyms, the coordination term and the entity layer per candidate with the same arithmetic as before; and the per-candidate path is untouched, still serving the case where the inverted index is disabled or the query carries identifiers. Search 10.67 to 8.35 ms (-21.8 percent, or -69.5 percent against 27.38 ms in 0.6.12), the production searchAdaptive path 12.52 to 10.16 ms (-18.9 percent), profiler samples 4,143.7 to 3,295.9 ms (-20.5 percent) with scanDoc gone from the top 25, index reuse still 0.69 ms per query. One cost, paid once: cold build 269 to about 300 ms, roughly 11 percent more, because each term stores two extra lists. One bug worth recording: the candidate list was not cleared at function entry, so the adaptive ruler swap pushed every candidate a second time and the finishing pass applied its factors twice, visible as an unchanged per-candidate path next to a shifted adaptive path. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty replies, and the 52-query real-store snapshot keeps all three tiers plus its two rank swaps. 0.6.17 trims the hit object before hydrating it. After 0.6.16 moved scoring onto the inverted index, search self time fell from 48 to 9 percent, and the most expensive remaining lines were no longer algorithm work but the receipt object literal itself: the scan loop built a fourteen-field hit for every candidate (level, title, content, importance plus five optional pass-through fields, with four conditional spreads), 134 to 176 ms per line and about 1.07 s over 300 queries, two thirds of the self time, while banding and trimming keep only the top k, so the plugin paid a full object for each of the thousands of entries destined to be dropped. Three changes keep semantics identical: the scan phase carries only what banding needs (subject, raw, cover, id, updated_at and score) plus an internal index, since band assignment and ordering read nothing else; after truncation the surviving k entries are hydrated back to the full object in the original key order, taking the score already on the lean object, because identifier bonus, level intent, assertion density and status digest have already been applied to it and recomputing would lose them, and replacing array elements in place rather than building a new array so the trimmed and rescueAdded properties survive; the explain and keepBand paths keep the full literal, since the former patches the object in place and the latter must keep the band for fusion. Search 8.35 to 3.5 ms (-58 percent, or -87 percent against 27.38 ms in 0.6.12), searchAdaptive 10.16 to 4.5 ms (-54 percent), profiler samples 3,295.9 to 1,808.2 ms, index reuse still 0.69 ms per query, cold build unchanged at 288 to 301 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty replies, and the 52-query real-store snapshot keeps all three tiers plus its two rank swaps. A new probe covers six checks: the lean path and the full path are byte-identical after dropping explain, key order included, the keepBand path matches after peeling internal fields, no internal fields leak while the array properties remain, optional fields are still omitted or passed through, and both paths agree on a large corpus. 0.6.18 drops Set from the candidate set. After 0.6.17 trimmed and hydrated hit objects, a hot search costs 3.49 ms, and the top functions are all per-query fixed costs over ten thousand entries, while the candidate set was still paying an avoidable price: the inverted-index path merged the entries hit by query terms and their co-occurrence expansions into a Set with two add rounds and iterated it, 137.4 ms or 7.6 percent per line, followed by the scoring function at 112.2 ms, all spent on hashing and iterator allocation, when the semantics need only two things: an index-to-seen lookup and first-seen ordering. Two changes, identical semantics: deduplication becomes a Uint8Array bitmap, with the two dedup sites reading if (candAt[di] === 0) { candAt[di] = 1; candList.push(di); }, one for query terms and one for expansions; the candidate table keeps first-seen order, and the scoring function loops by index, with length normalization, the coverage table, the candidate array and both null checks, first pass and rescaled pass, now testing the candidate table. The fallback is untouched: with the inverted index off or an identifier in the query the bitmap is null and the full scan runs. Bit-identical because first-seen order is exactly the insertion order of the set, the bitmap answers only seen-or-not, and push preserves order, so the candidate array layout, scan order, floating point addition order and receipt order are unchanged. Search 3.49 to 3.01 ms (-13.7 percent, or -89 percent against 27.377 ms in 0.6.12), searchAdaptive 4.568 to 4.54 ms, profiler samples 1,808.2 to 1,678.4 ms, and the candidate block left the top twenty. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty replies, and the 52-query real-store snapshot keeps all three tiers plus its two rank swaps. A new probe covers six checks: the seven source facts including that Set has left the candidate block, a 200-case comparison of bitmap union against set union, bit-identical results with the inverted index on and off, that the synonym expansion path is really exercised because the trimmed counter goes from undefined to one while order is unchanged and only scores differ, an empty query never yields NaN, and 300 entries times 30 queries stay bit-identical on both paths. 0.6.19 removes the sort from band assignment. After 0.6.18 switched the candidate set to a bitmap, a hot search costs 2.98 ms, and the runner-up function is still band assignment at 235.6 ms or 14.0 percent, where the single most expensive line is the bulk sort at 164.9 ms, seventy percent of that function: the work is to walk ten thousand raw scores from high to low and open a new band whenever a value falls below 0.85 times the previous anchor, yet the anchor chain only consumes the distinct sorted values and was paying a comparison sort for every entry first. The cause is that band assignment needs a descending walk, not a total order. Three changes, identical semantics: the bucket key is the high thirty-two bits of the IEEE bit pattern shifted right by sixteen, since for non-negative finite doubles the bit pattern orders like the value, a sixteen-bit bucket is 6.25 percent wide, two values in one bucket differ by at least a factor of 0.941, far above one minus 0.85, so a bucket holds at most one anchor and its maximum suffices without sorting; counting sort gathers runs and then one walk over bucket numbers from high to low picks, per bucket segment, the largest value still below the threshold as the next anchor and skips a bucket whose whole segment is above it; bucket zero is special-cased because zero and all subnormals share it with no bound on relative spread, so that segment is copied out, sorted, and walked with the same chain, which is what makes corpora spanning ten to the plus or minus three hundred line up. One fallback: on a big-endian host the bit pattern no longer orders like the value, so the old sorted chain runs, sorting only the first n entries because the buffer is reused and its tail holds the previous round. Bit-identical because the chain definition is unchanged, buckets only change the order in which values are read, a bucket cannot hold a second anchor, the maximum is taken instead of a sorted value, bucket zero is really sorted, and the binary search in band assignment is untouched. Search 2.982 to 2.52 ms (-15.4 percent, or -90.8 percent against 27.377 ms in 0.6.12), searchAdaptive 4.105 to 3.51 ms, band assignment 235.6 to 74.0 ms (14.0 to 4.9 percent), the new helper itself only 28.5 ms or 1.9 percent, profiler samples 1,678.4 to 1,520.9 ms, and cold index builds stay at 292 to 299 ms. Ranking is bit-identical: LoCoMo hit@1 0.3932, hit@5 0.6192, hit@10 0.6924, hit@20 0.7511, MRR 0.4958, recall@20 0.6322, zero empty replies, and the 52-query real-store snapshot keeps all three tiers plus its two rank swaps. A new probe covers seven checks: source shape including that the bulk sort has left the threshold path, bit-identical anchors against the sorted chain on five hundred random corpora with zeros, duplicates, subnormals and values spanning ten to the plus or minus three hundred, a same-bucket ratio floor of 0.85 with a measured worst case of 0.943627, degenerate corpora, band-by-band comparison with identified rows excluded from the chain, a reused buffer that never bleeds, and bucket-number facts where zero and the smallest subnormal land in bucket zero and 1.0 lands in 16368. 0.6.20 removes the weak-map lookup from signature checking. After 0.6.19 dropped the sort from band assignment, a hot search costs 2.52 ms and the top function became the per-document signature reader at 265.5 ms or 16.4 percent: all it answers is whether this corpus is still the corpus from a moment ago, so it walks the document array once, compares eight fields per entry, folds them into one total signature, and uses that signature as the key of the search-index cache. The per-entry record it folds comes from a weak map keyed by the document object; the field comparison is cheap, the read is not. A ten-thousand-entry corpus pays ten thousand hash lookups per question, while a second visit to the same array finds every entry at the same index: what is needed is the previous verdict by index, what was paid is a hash lookup by object, and the same question even computed the signature twice. Two changes plus three things not to touch: first, an aligned row cache whose weak-map key is the document array itself, holding an array of rows aligned one-to-one with indices, each row holding the very same per-entry record object rather than a copy, so the read becomes an indexed element access; second, rows are only allocated on the second visit, because callers in the real store often hand in a freshly built array, where allocating ten thousand empty slots would be a regression. Untouched: the folding order, so the XOR and multiply still run in document order and the signature stays bit-identical, otherwise the cache key and the signature probes fail together; the counting contract, so a row hit still records a hit and a reuse and entries that are not objects, or whose fields are not scalars, or whose keywords hold non-scalars, keep an empty row and are computed fresh, otherwise two differently shaped dirty entries would collapse into one; and the path for non-array iterables, since anything other than an array has no index alignment to speak of. The question now computes the signature once and shares it between the cache key and the self-check. Readings on ten thousand same-shape entries over three hundred questions, median of three: search 2.522 to 2.042 ms, down 19.0 percent and 92.5 percent below 0.6.12 at 27.377 ms; searchAdaptive, which is what the product calls, 3.51 to 2.59 ms, down 26.1 percent; total profile samples 1,624.0 to 1,433.5 ms; the per-entry function left the leaderboard; the fresh-array path moved from 2.579 to 2.604 ms inside noise, so it does not regress; cold build stays at 291 to 297 ms. Not one answer moved: on LoCoMo, ten samples, five thousand eight hundred eighty-two turns, one thousand nine hundred eighty-six questions, the old and new engines agree on zero mismatches across the top twenty per question, and the real store keeps its three tiers at 0.921, 0.417 and 0.500 with both rank shifts intact. A new probe adds six checks: the shape, four thousand and eighteen bit-identical comparisons between the row-cached pass and the fresh-array pass, an identical counting contract on both paths, eight kinds of edits all visible, three consecutive calls agreeing and a copy agreeing, and dirty entries staying distinct. Its second check first failed for a measurement reason rather than a semantic one: two paths sharing one batch of document objects let the first fill the per-entry cache, so each path now gets its own same-shape corpus. 0.6.21 removes the per-character Unicode regex from lexical classification. After 0.6.20 moved signature checking to an aligned row cache, a hot search costs 2.04 ms, and unfolding the function view by line shows the costliest single line is not in search but in the small function that only answers whether a code point is Han, alphanumeric, or punctuation: 71.4 ms plus 16.2 ms, 88.7 ms or 6.2 percent for the function. The cause is plain: the verdict depends only on the code point, so it is a table lookup, yet the hot path runs two Unicode property regexes per code point, once per code point while tokenizing and again at every segment boundary, over the same corpus of ten thousand entries for every question. The fixes, plus three things not to touch: first, a code point table with three values for blank, Han, and alphanumeric, built by the same two regexes scanning their own contiguous runs, so equivalence is constructed rather than hand-transcribed; second, build it lazily, once, on the first classification, sixty-four kilobytes, then a single indexed read, while astral code points and lone surrogates still take the original regex path; tokenizing compares numbers instead of strings and the exported string classifier stays as a thin wrapper under the same name. Untouched: the table must be scanned out of the regexes, since the katakana prolonged sound mark and the ideographic iteration mark belong to common script and the alphanumeric class admits extra letters, so hand transcription always misses; the priority stays Han first then alphanumeric, with alphanumeric only filling still-blank cells; and astral code points stay out of the table, because it covers only the basic plane and anything outside must take the regex path or a surrogate pair would be split into two half code points. Readings, ten thousand entries and three hundred questions, median of three: search 2.042 to 2.000 ms, adaptive 2.593 to 2.528 ms, cold build 292 to 233.5 ms, total sampled time 1433.5 to 1337.0 ms, and the classifier drops off the profile. The real gain is in the cold build, not the hot question. Answers are unchanged: the real-store fifty-two question suite keeps 0.921, 0.417, and 0.500 with the same rank movements, and LoCoMo with ten samples, 5882 turns, and 1986 questions matches on the top twenty for every question across old and new engines. New probes: probe-lex with six checks, including an exhaustive comparison over all 1112064 code points and a cell-by-cell comparison of the 65536-cell table. 0.6.22 stops tokenizing the same fields twice while building the index. After 0.6.21 replaced the lexical classifier with a code point table, a hot search settled near two milliseconds, and unfolding the function view by line moves the cost to the cold build: index construction is over ten percent of the sample, and the five costliest lines all sit on the tokenize-and-count chain. Two causes: the same fields are tokenized twice, since the body is tokenized once for one token list and again for its length account, the title once for each of two tables, and keywords carry two identical expressions in two places; and every entry allocates a dedupe set, so each entry-term pair pays a membership probe plus an insert, four hash lookups per pair counting the frequency update, only to answer whether this term is new in this entry. Two fixes and three things not to touch: first, split tokenizing into a segment pass that only cuts runs by code point and is pure, and a finish pass that decides English normalization from the composition of the whole list, with the exported function becoming a one line wrapper; the build then tokenizes title and body once each and fills the body tokens, the body length account and the title set in place from those two segment lists, while keywords are finished once and the other two tables derive from it. Second, the dedupe set goes away and the frequency map itself answers first occurrence, since both writes only ever increment. Untouched: finishing must run once over the whole list because it looks at the composition ratio, and the first implementation finished each segment separately and was caught by the differential harness with fifty two mismatches, since a Latin heavy title loses stop words and gets stemmed while the same title concatenated with Chinese body is no longer Latin heavy; segmenting is interchangeable only because blanks and punctuation never merge across words; and the frequency map only grows, which is what makes dropping the dedupe set safe. Readings, same process alternating old and new, median of nine: cold build 236.28 to 200.3 ms, minus 15.2 percent, hot search 1.849 to 1.878 ms within noise, official table cold build 233.5 to 204 through 221 ms, total sampled 1337 to 1254.2 ms, minus 6.2 percent. No answer moved: the differential harness over ten synthetic plus one thousand four hundred fifty one real rounds times nine option sets plus two real stores reports zero mismatches in two hundred seventy seven checks across eleven rounds; LoCoMo ten samples, five thousand eight hundred eighty two rounds, one thousand nine hundred eighty six questions, top twenty compared question by question, zero differences; and the real store keeps 0.921, 0.417 and 0.500 with the same two rank swaps. New criterion probe-cold with six checks: eleven source shapes, fourteen segment pairs, fourteen finish pairs including a mixed counterexample, five tables against the old expressions over twelve by four branches, determinism across two paths, and eleven degenerate cases. 0.6.23 stops the co occurrence table and the session topic pass from doing the same work twice. After 0.6.22 cleaned up the tokenizing chain, a cold build profile put the remaining cost squarely on co occurrence learning and session topics: line by line the costliest spot is the frequency bump for a word pair, then a character by character shared Han lookup, then the two Han test expressions, then the session topic pass that walks every token again just to count how many sessions a term spans, then the row fetch. Three causes: the same word pair is tested for shared Han over and over even though the test is pure, since the project layer pairs each entry with every word in the project union and repeats a pair dozens of times, paying two expressions and a character scan each time; each entry tokenizes its keyword list twice in one pass, once for the same entry layer and again for the project layer, which for comma or serialized keyword strings parses the same string twice; and the session topic pass walks the same tokens twice, once only to count sessions per term by building a set per session, then again to accumulate frequency per session over the same array. Three fixes plus one, with the result untouched: first, remember the shared Han verdict per word pair in one table behind a closure, computing the test only on a miss and writing the boolean back, with both layers going through that closure while the weight is still decided by the caller; second, tokenize each entry keyword list once and index into it from both layers; third, hoist the project layer row fetch out of the inner loop without changing when rows are created, so key insertion order stays bit identical; fourth, compute session topics in a single pass, with one stamped map keyed by session ordinal replacing one set per session, filling frequency and session counts together and skipping sessions under the threshold. Readings: seven alternating rounds in one process, cold build two hundred one point zero six to one hundred seventy seven point two one milliseconds, down eleven point nine percent, hot search unchanged within noise, the cold build profile sample nine hundred seventy point five to eight hundred nineteen point six milliseconds, down fifteen point five percent, and the shared Han test drops off the board entirely. Not one answer moved: the old and new builds agree across twenty synthetic documents times eleven switch combinations plus one thousand four hundred fifty one real rounds times three combinations, plus a direct comparison of the co occurrence learn flag on both sides, four hundred sixty two checks with zero mismatches, matching co occurrence key order, token lists, postings, frequencies, document frequencies, title sets, keyword sets and body strings; real question comparison shows no difference; the reference library keeps its three tiers and both rank shifts. New checks add four co occurrence probe cases and one session topic differential: token lists read once counted by getter, the table matching a naive ruler key by key value by value order by order, sessions over the threshold appending the same tail, sessions under the threshold appending nothing. 0.6.24 removes the second lookup the index build kept paying. After 0.6.23 cleaned up the co occurrence layer, a cold build profile moved the cost into the postings loop and the first line of tokenizing: line by line the costliest spot is the document frequency read and write back, then the closing pass that looks each term up in postings again, then the two set membership tests while writing field positions, then the first sight counter write, then tokenizing that split the whole string into single characters, then the session topic stamp map. Three causes: the first sight of a term in a document is recorded three times, once to detect it, once to count document frequency and once to fetch the postings entry, while document frequency is exactly the length of that entry document array, so the extra record is pure waste; the closing pass looks the term up a second time only to recover a pointer that was already in hand at first sight; and tokenizing split the whole string into single character objects just to classify by index, creating garbage that later slicing joined back together and that the collector then had to reclaim, plus a fourth cause in that the session topic stamp map was a second ledger, since the frequency map is already new for every session and stamping every term costs one more lookup. Three fixes plus one, with the result untouched: first, remember the postings entry at first sight by index into one reused array and read it back by index in the closing pass, clearing only the length between documents instead of allocating an array per document; second, derive document frequency from the length of that entry document array and keep the inline counting only on the branch where postings are disabled; third, tokenize by index, judging code point width so astral characters count as two units, advancing segment boundaries over runs of one class, slicing directly, and still forming Han bigrams inside a segment; fourth, reuse the frequency map as the session topic dedupe, so a missing entry means first sight in that session and the stamp map and its ordinal both disappear. Readings: seven alternating rounds in one process, cold build from one hundred seventy four point four six down to one hundred forty nine point two seven milliseconds, a fourteen point four percent cut, with query time inside the noise; the official table moved its three cold builds to one hundred forty seven point five one, one hundred forty six point six eight and one hundred fifty seven point zero nine milliseconds, and total time into the six hundred twenty millisecond range, while the cold profile dropped its total samples from eight hundred nineteen point six to seven hundred forty one point seven milliseconds, with tokenizing from eighty seven point one to sixty one point seven, session topics from eighty three point nine to fifty four point seven and the index build from two hundred forty point six to one hundred ninety five point eight. No answer moved: the real library triple and the two rank shifts are unchanged, one thousand nine hundred eighty six questions compare with zero differences, the old and new index builds agree on four hundred sixty two checks across twenty synthetic documents times eleven switch groups and one thousand four hundred fifty one real turns times three switch groups, and tokenizing agrees on thirty seven adversarial strings and seven thousand eight hundred sixty eight real turns. Two new cold build checks and six index shape checks were added. Self-checked by 50 suites / 3,827 executable assertions in about 220 seconds.
description.zh: 一个记忆插件顶三个：8 个统一 memory_* 工具 + 一段 1,235 字符常驻注入，主库仍是 meow-memory 的七层 SQLite，星图退成可重建的索引。工具 schema 56,759 B → 13,567 B（−76.1%），常驻注入 4,085 → 1,235 字符（−69.8%）。能力一条没砍：写入先落主库，连不上星图的连线排队不丢，设置页改完即刻生效、不用重启。0.4.0 又加了查询分解、写入巩固、自动取代与通胀体检、实体层、以及从你自己的 keywords 学出来的共现扩词——每一件都有开关，也都有开/关对照读数；0.5.0 用 CJK 词形桥让换说法也能落地。0.6.0 让打分随库规模自适应：660 条快照上照抄 hit@1 0.895 → 0.921、换说法 0.333 → 0.417、误伤 0，每条命中顺带带 `status`。0.6.1 把「三棵树没同步」做成一条命令（`tools/sync-trees.mjs`，默认只体检、从不删除），用两条静态正则钉住自适应 idf 的接线点（判据全绿但行为回退这种沉默故障过不去），并修掉一个维护脚本的 `%20` 路径 bug——引擎字节未变。0.6.2 修的是一个把「有」说成「没有」的缺陷：噪声地板剔掉了唯一能命中的词、留下库里根本不存在（df=0）的词顶位，1,531 条英文问句里 8 条回执为空；处方只救被噪声地板剔掉的词（虚词一个都不救），空回 0.52% → 0，hit@1/5/10/20、MRR 与 660 条快照三档读数逐位不变。0.6.3 让答案是可复现的：分数并列时以前会退回语料顺序（V8 稳定排序），同一个问句能因为存储布局不同给出两套前十；定序梯子现在末尾是「更新得更晚的在前」+ id 自然序，自适应 idf 挑簇不再按数组下标破平，整条链上也没有 localeCompare——所有读数逐位不变。0.6.4 修的是「一个汉字也是问题」：分词只产二元组，一个汉字的问句切出来是空数组，检索的第一道门就把「切不出词」当成「没有」，于是 `读`/`钱`/`花` 这类最直白的问法永远空手。现在只在「切不出词 + 单个汉字」时按原文子串在标题、正文与关键词里找一次，仍走同一套定序；英文停用词与标点一个都不放行。所有读数逐位不变——修的是可达性，不是排序。0.6.5 修的是「标点也是人打的」：0.6.4 的单字兜底只认「正好一个码点」，可人问一个字的时候问号几乎从不缺席——`读？`、`钱。`、`花！`、`「读」` 一个都回不来。现在把标点与空白剥掉再数，剥完正好剩一个汉字才走兜底，汉字之外只许标点或空白；字母、数字、符号一律不放行，同一个字重复按一个算。所有读数又是一位没动——修的仍是可达性，不是排序。0.6.6 修的是「脏记忆不许把整次检索打成异常」：`docText` 里的 `...d.keywords` 遇上缺字段 / `null` / 逗号串（导入行、别的插件写的行、调用方自拼的 docs）会抛 `TypeError: d.keywords is not iterable`——不是少一条命中，是整次检索一个回执都拿不回来。现在 keywords 统一走 `kwList`：数组、逗号顿号串、JSON 串都认，`docText`、打分面的 `kwToks`/`kwSets`、`keywordHitScore` 与索引签名全走它（逗号串的关键词从此真进 tf-idf）。读数一位没动，修的是可达性。0.6.7 修的是「一条坏行不许把整次检索打成异常」：`docs` 里混进一条 `null` / `undefined` / 标量（半写的行、导入截断、调用方把 id 列表当 docs），`docText` 的 `d.title` 会抛 `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'title')`；`docs` 整个不是数组时死在 `docs.length`。现在两个入口都过闸 `liveDocs(docs)`：非数组回空、逐条问「是不是对象」、脏了才过滤，干净数组原样返回同一引用（索引缓存的键是内容签名，不靠身份，缓存不会被打掉）；全是坏行时回空，不把 `null` 当一条记忆打分。读数一位没动。0.6.8 治的是判据自己的寿命：版本号、支数、断言总数、耗时预算每版都在动，写成等值就每升一版必红一次（`0.2.31→35` 四遍版本等值、`0.6.2→0.6.7` 每版手工抬 `steps.length === 35 → 36` 并连带改两处手抄的「N 支 / M 条」）。现在支数是地板 `SUITE_FLOOR`（只许加不许减，减一支立刻红、加一支不必动判据），文档里「现在」的数由探针读基线合计自动对账，历史里程碑冻结自己那版的数字，版本阶梯按版本号比。引擎一个字节没动，读数逐位相同。0.6.9 先量了尺子：0.3.0 起所有对外读数都是单次、单序量出来的（语料按库里顺序、问句按夹具顺序、跑一遍取一个数），而这一路正是拿这些单次数否决过三个候选（英文词形归一、MMR、覆盖率重排）——量尺若对顺序敏感，那些「负数」里就掺着量尺自己的噪声。现在 `tools/probe-rigor.mjs` 钉住七条：连跑 3 次三档读数逐位相同（std = 0）、语料倒序、三种打乱（seed 3/11/42）、问句倒序、独立 scorer 交叉验、进程内注入「同分按语料序」的偏置必红（A/B 互换第一名命中 23→15）、分档口径 45/14/10。真库样张 69 问 hit@1 0.9565 / hit@3 0.9855 / MRR 0.9686，三次与换序后一个字都不差。引擎一个字节没动，LoCoMo 与真库读数逐位不变。0.6.10 治的是每问一次的固定开销：索引缓存的键是内容签名，而「库没变」这个答案几乎每回都成立，代价却每次全额付。四条同构语料（660 / 2,000 / 5,000 / 10,000）上签名占一次热检索 28.8%–30.6%（0.96 / 2.84 / 7.04 / 14.16 ms）。改后按条记账：WeakMap 以 doc 为键存条级 32 位哈希与字段值快照，逐字段比较值（不是对象身份），全等才复用；条级哈希从滚动值里拆出来才能缓存；判不出有没有变的形状走直算。读数：签名 0.062 / 0.189 / 0.528 / 1.198 ms（15×）、占比降到 2.8%–3.5%，一次热检索 3.24→2.18、9.67→6.80、23.0→15.3、49.2→37.6 ms。排序一个字节没动，LoCoMo 与真库读数逐位不变。0.6.11 接着算固定开销：把热检索剩下的钱按通道拆开点名，最贵的一块是原样匹配——为了回答「这条里有没有原样出现这个标识符」，它每问一次都把整库拼成一份小写大字符串（id + project + title + content + keywords），10,000 条就是 2.03 MB，占一次热检索 35.7%–50.6%（660/2,000/5,000/10,000 条实测）；再拆一层，造串 5.78 ms 而真正的扫描只要 0.51 ms。改后 haystack 跟切词表一样搬进索引、按条懒建并记账（built / reused），问句里没有标识符时一条都不建；顺手补掉 0.6.10 的洞：haystack 含 project 而 project 从不进签名，搬进索引后就会「改 project 拿旧串答新库」，故 project 补进签名与值比较。读数：全量检索 2.04→1.62、5.04→4.20、11.88→9.12、24.45→18.82 ms（−20.6% / −16.7% / −23.2% / −23.0%），原样匹配份额降到 18.6%–34.9%。排序一个字节没动：LoCoMo 与真库读数逐位不变。0.6.12 接着算固定开销，这一版治的是最后一步定序。顺着 0.6.10 的签名账与 0.6.11 的原样匹配账往下，用 --cpu-prof 按函数归因（10,000 条 / 300 问），最大的一块是 bandize：为了交出前十名，它对全量命中排了两遍，先按 _raw 排一遍定档，再按档位、分数、更新时间、id 排一遍定序，而三个调用点之后都只取前 k 条，等于每次检索都在为 5 条答案给 9,995 条陪跑排队，定序占一次热检索 40.3%（约 11ms/问），比扫文档还贵。改后档号直接写在条目自己身上（撤掉每问新建的 Map）、比较器抽成 orderOf 一条梯子（档位 → 分数 → 更新得更晚的在前 → id 自然序，全序与堆两路共用）、bandize 收 limit 并用有界最大堆选前 k（根是入选里最差的那条，更好的才顶掉根），want 不小于总数时整段退回原来的全量排序，小库与大 k 行为逐位不变；截断之后才落 _band 与 explain.band，并删掉临时字段。读数：search 27.377→19.985 ms（−27.0%）、产品走的 searchAdaptive 31.086→23.097 ms（−25.7%），定序份额 40.3%→21.5%（orderOf 自身只占 0.9%），索引复用仍是 0.751ms/问、冷建索引 270.7ms 未动。答案一位没动：前 k 与全量排完再切逐位相同（500 组随机语料 × 六种 k 对拍，判据探针自带老实现作参考），返回条数合计 1,500 不变，LoCoMo 与真库 52 问读数逐位不变。0.6.13 继续算固定开销，这一版治的是定档。0.6.12 把定序截到前 k 之后，--cpu-prof 复测（10,000 条 / 300 问，单次 19.99ms）剩下最大的一块仍在那次只为定档的全量排序上：bandize 里 hits.slice().sort((a, b) => b[rawKey] - a[rawKey])，占一次热检索 21.5%（bandize 10.9% 加内部 raw 比较器 10.6%），等于为一堆注定进不了前 k 的条目逐对调比较器、逐对读对象字段。而档号其实只由排序后的不同 raw 值决定，处方三步、口径一字不改：把 raw 抄进 Float64Array，用 TypedArray 原生 的老全量排序 setBandsBySort；指认档照旧恒负一档且不进链。读数：search 19.985→16.329 ms（−18.3%）、产品走的 searchAdaptive 23.097→18.812 ms（−18.6%），定档那一块 21.5%→7.8%（阈值链 7.0% 加 bandize 0.8%），索引复用仍是 0.703ms/问、冷建索引 之后，函数视图只剩在干活的样（search 自证 45.8%、scanDoc 17.8%），换成行级归因（读 cpuprofile 的 positionTicks）才看见病灶：delete h._lv 一行 791.5ms，delete h._vb 与 delete h._sr 另 353ms，总采样 5,671.8ms 里 1.14s（约两成）花在把刚挂上去的临时值摘下来。根因是 hit 对象上四个先用后摘的中间值（原样命中位、句式比、层级意图、断言密度）用完靠 delete 收场，而 delete 会把对象打进字典模式，此后它每一次属性读写（包括 0.6.13 刚优化的 bandize 里那句 h._raw）都走哈希表——省四次赋值，赔整条热路。处方两条、口径一字不改：四个临时值改放与 hits 同下标的平行数组（push 紧挨 hits.push，收尾按 hi 读），回执对象字段集合一个不增一个不减；idf 每一趟记一次账（同一趟里 idf 只由词的 df 决定，是常量，改成每问一个 idfCache 加 idfAt，值逐位相同，只是不再重复算 Math.log），自适应 idf 换尺子时清账，否则第二遍会拿旧尺子的数。顺带收掉每问一次的 raw.slice（只在 explain 开时才留）与 Math.max 展开（10k 参数改成循环，用非大于判据保住 NaN 传播）。读数：search 16.329→11.567 ms（−29.2%），相对 0.6.12 的 27.377 累计 −57.7%；产品走的 searchAdaptive 18.812→13.520 ms（−28.1%）；热路上 delete 零处，索引复用 0.679ms/问、冷建 275ms。答案一个字节没动：LoCoMo 1,531 问 hit@1 0.3932、hit@5 0.6192、hit@10 0.6924、hit@20 0.7511、MRR 0.4958、recall@20 0.6322、空回 0，真库 52 问与 0.6.13 逐位相同。0.6.15 这一版治的是覆盖度不再逐条重算。0.6.14 把 delete 那 1.14s 收掉之后，函数视图仍只剩在干活的样（search 自证 40.6%、scanDoc
